title: You Keep Calling It “Waiting on God”—But Deep Down, You Know You’re Afraid to Obey.
paragraphs: You Keep Calling It “Waiting on God”—But Deep Down, You Know You’re Afraid to Obey.
Sometimes the silence you are blaming on God is happening after He has already spoken—and what feels like spiritual patience may actually be fear wearing the clothes of faith.
There is a prayer you can keep praying long after you already know the answer.
“Lord, show me what to do.”
You whisper it in the morning.
You pray it before sleeping.
You ask for confirmation.
Then another confirmation.
Then a sermon.
Then a sign.
Then “peace.”
Then the perfect timing.
And because all of this sounds spiritual, almost nobody questions it.
Not even you.
But somewhere underneath all those prayers is a possibility you have been trying not to touch:
What if God has already made the next faithful step clear?
What if the problem is no longer that you do not know?
What if you are afraid of what obedience might cost you?
That question hurts because fear knows how to speak Christian.
Fear does not always scream, “I refuse to obey God.”
Sometimes fear whispers,
“I’m still praying about it.”
“I’m waiting on the Lord.”
“I just need another confirmation.”
“I don’t have peace yet.”
“Maybe this isn’t the right season.”
And sometimes those statements are completely legitimate. Scripture does call believers to pray, seek wisdom, wait upon the Lord, test what they hear, and refuse reckless decisions.
There are seasons when waiting is obedience.
But there are also moments when waiting becomes a respectable name for delay.
That distinction matters.
Because James writes something brutally simple:
—James 1:22, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing:
“Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταὶ παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτούς.”
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai paralogizomenoi heautous.
In context, James is not attacking careful discernment. He is confronting the dangerous gap between receiving God’s Word and actually living according to it.
The word translated “doers,” ποιηταί (poiētai), speaks of those who do, make, or practice something.
Not merely admirers of the Word.
Not collectors of sermons.
Not people endlessly fascinated by biblical truth.
Doers.
And then comes the uncomfortable word:
παραλογιζόμενοι (paralogizomenoi).
Deceiving yourselves.
Misreasoning.
Drawing a false conclusion through faulty reasoning.
That means James recognizes something frightening about the human heart:
You can hear truth and still construct an argument convincing enough to make disobedience feel reasonable.
You can even make it sound spiritual.
And maybe that is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you already know you need to forgive someone.
But you keep waiting until you “feel ready.”
Maybe you know you need to confess what you have hidden.
But you are terrified of what honesty could cost.
Maybe you know that relationship keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you know the business practice is dishonest.
Maybe you know the apology needs to happen.
Maybe you know you need to stop returning to that secret sin.
Maybe Scripture has already settled the moral question, but you keep asking God to give you a different answer because the biblical one is painful.
Maybe obedience could cost you comfort.
Reputation.
Money.
Control.
A relationship.
An opportunity.
Someone’s approval.
And suddenly “waiting on God” becomes safer than walking with God.
Read that again.
Because there is a difference between waiting for God and waiting instead of obeying God.
Scripture honors the first.
It does not authorize the second.
Abraham knew something about this.
Genesis 12 records God telling Abram to leave his country, kindred, and father’s house for a land God would show him.
Imagine that conversation happening today.
“But Lord, where exactly?”
“What is the five-year plan?”
“What happens financially?”
“Can You show me the entire route first?”
“What if my family thinks I’ve lost my mind?”
“Can I have three confirmations?”
But Scripture gives us a stunning sentence:
“So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him…”
—Genesis 12:4, KJV
He did not possess the entire map.
He possessed a word from God sufficient for the step God required.
That is faith.
Biblical faith is not knowing everything that will happen.
It is trusting the God who knows everything that will happen.
And perhaps this is why obedience can feel terrifying.
We want God to reveal enough of tomorrow that obedience today no longer requires trust.
But then it would not be faith.
Hebrews 11:8 says of Abraham:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Notice the order.
Called.
Obeyed.
Went.
Not knowing.
We often want the order reversed.
Knowing.
Understanding.
Feeling safe.
Receiving guarantees.
Then obeying.
But faith sometimes walks while questions are still unanswered.
This does not mean every strong feeling, inner impression, dream, coincidence, or personal desire is God's command.
That distinction is crucial.
Christians are not commanded to obey every thought that enters their minds.
We test everything against Scripture.
We seek wisdom.
We pray.
We welcome mature biblical counsel.
And when Scripture has not prescribed a specific choice—Which job? Which city? Which house? Which legitimate opportunity?—careful discernment may be exactly what faithfulness requires.
But when God has already spoken clearly in His Word, “I’m waiting for confirmation” can become dangerous.
You do not need another sign to determine whether you should repent of known sin.
You do not need another prophecy to discover whether Christians are called to forgive.
You do not need another dream to determine whether dishonesty is wrong.
You do not need a mystical feeling before loving your enemy.
You do not need perfect emotional certainty before doing what Scripture has plainly commanded.
Sometimes we are not waiting for clarity.
We are waiting for obedience to become painless.
And it may never become painless.
Ask Jesus.
Gethsemane destroys the shallow idea that obedience always feels peaceful.
Jesus knew exactly what obedience would cost.
He was not confused about His mission.
He was approaching betrayal, humiliation, torture, crucifixion, and the bearing of sin according to the saving purpose of God.
Matthew records Him praying:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
—Matthew 26:39, KJV
Do not rush past that.
Jesus did not teach us that faithful obedience means the absence of anguish.
He showed us perfect obedience in the presence of anguish.
The Son submitted to the Father even when the road before Him led to a cross.
And because He did…
sinners like us have hope.
This is where Christianity separates itself from motivational self-improvement.
The Gospel is not simply:
“Stop being afraid and obey harder.”
If that were the message, frightened sinners would merely receive another burden.
The Gospel begins with what Christ has done.
Jesus obeyed where we have failed.
Jesus remained faithful where we have compromised.
Jesus went to the cross for sinners—including procrastinating, frightened, excuse-making, self-deceiving sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the scandal of grace is that the person who finally admits, “Lord, I have been hiding behind excuses,” does not discover a Savior standing far away with folded arms.
The repentant sinner discovers Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in victory.
Full of truth.
Full of grace.
Calling us out of darkness.
Not so we can remain unchanged, but so grace can produce what fear never could.
A surrendered life.
This is why grace must never become another excuse for disobedience.
Grace does not say, “Your rebellion does not matter.”
Grace says, “Your rebellion mattered enough that Christ shed His blood—and His mercy is great enough to forgive you and transform you.”
Jesus does not merely forgive us from something.
He calls us into something.
Follow Me.
That invitation has always carried a cost.
Peter had to leave nets.
Matthew had to leave the tax booth.
Zacchaeus could not encounter Christ and continue treating money the same way.
Paul could not meet the risen Jesus and continue persecuting His church.
Again and again, grace interrupts a life and produces movement.
Not perfect movement.
Not fearless movement.
But surrendered movement.
And perhaps that is what you have been avoiding.
You keep asking God to remove the fear before you obey.
Perhaps courage will come differently.
Perhaps courage will meet you while your hands are still shaking.
Peter did not discover that water was solid before stepping out of the boat.
Abraham did not receive the entire itinerary before leaving.
The servants at Cana filled the waterpots before they saw what Jesus would do.
Obedience frequently begins before outcomes are visible.
And there is something else you need to hear.
Delayed obedience can become dangerous because repeated resistance can train your heart to become comfortable with conviction.
The first time God’s Word confronts something in you, it hurts.
The tenth time, perhaps a little less.
Eventually, you can learn how to hear a sermon about your exact compromise, say “Amen,” feel convicted for five minutes, and continue living exactly the same way.
That is why James does not merely warn about ignorance.
He warns about self-deception.
You can become so familiar with truth that hearing it begins to feel like obeying it.
You highlight the verse.
Save the sermon.
Post the quote.
Cry during worship.
And still refuse the thing Christ is putting His finger on.
That is terrifying.
Because proximity to truth is not the same thing as surrender to truth.
James continues with the picture of someone looking into a mirror and then walking away, immediately forgetting what he saw.
Scripture does not merely give us information about God.
It exposes us before God.
And sometimes the reflection is uncomfortable.
Maybe the mirror is showing you fear.
Maybe pride.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe a relationship you have made into an idol.
Maybe a secret habit you keep promising to surrender “eventually.”
Maybe an apology you owe.
Maybe restitution needs to happen.
Maybe you need to ask for help because the private battle is becoming stronger than your private resistance.
Maybe your next act of obedience is not dramatic at all.
Maybe it is one phone call.
One confession.
One boundary.
One conversation.
One deleted number.
One honest sentence.
One act of forgiveness.
One decision to stop hiding.
One trembling prayer:
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And maybe you are afraid that if you surrender, everything will fall apart.
But what if the thing falling apart is the prison you have mistaken for protection?
What if obedience does cost something?
It probably will.
Jesus never advertised discipleship as painless.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
—Matthew 16:24, KJV
A cross is not comfortable.
Self-denial is not comfortable.
Repentance is not comfortable.
Confession can be humiliating.
Forgiveness can feel unfair.
Leaving sin can feel like losing something you cannot live without.
But sin has always lied about what it gives and hidden what it takes.
Jesus tells the truth about both the cost and the destination.
He calls us to Himself.
And this is the moment where you need to stop thinking about everybody else who should read this.
Not your spouse.
Not your friend.
Not the lukewarm Christian you have been worried about.
You.
What have you been calling “waiting on God” that may actually be fear of obeying what God has already made clear?
Do not answer publicly if doing so would expose something that should remain private.
But answer God.
Be painfully honest.
“Lord, I am scared.”
That is a prayer God can work with.
“Lord, I know what Your Word says, but I don't know if I have the courage.”
Bring Him that.
“Lord Jesus, I have been asking for another answer because I don't like the answer Scripture already gave me.”
Bring Him that too.
Repentance begins in truth.
You do not have to impress Jesus with religious language.
He already knows.
He knows what you are afraid of losing.
He knows the conversation you dread.
He knows the consequences you cannot predict.
He knows how long you have been postponing this.
And He knows every failure that brought you here.
Still, grace calls.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that blesses our hiding.
Grace that opens the prison door and says,
“Come out.”
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment when another excuse was forming.
Maybe tonight you were going to tell yourself, “Next week.”
Maybe after one more prayer.
One more sign.
One more Sunday.
One more confirmation.
One more comfortable delay.
But perhaps your next prayer should not be,
“God, tell me what to do.”
Perhaps it should be,
“God, give me courage to obey what You have already shown me through Your Word.”
That changes everything.
And please understand this carefully:
You are not saved because you finally become courageous enough.
You are not justified before God by accumulating impressive acts of obedience.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works that give us grounds for boasting, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But the passage does not stop there.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace saves.
And saving grace transforms.
We do not obey so Christ will love us enough to save us.

We obey because Christ is Lord, because His grace has captured us, and because genuine faith cannot be content forever with merely hearing the voice of the Shepherd while continually refusing to follow Him.
So if fear has been hiding behind spiritual vocabulary, bring it into the light.
No performance.
No pretending.
No religious costume.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I am afraid.”
Then ask Him for strength.
Open Scripture.
Seek wise biblical counsel where discernment is genuinely needed.
Make sure what you are calling “God's will” actually agrees with God's Word.
And when Scripture has made your responsibility clear…
take the next faithful step.
Not every step for the next twenty years.
The next one.
You may still tremble.
Obey trembling.
You may still cry.
Obey crying.
You may not know how everything ends.
Obey trusting Christ with the ending.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding behind spiritual language, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can make a simple confession of dependence:
Let other believers know they are not the only ones trembling between conviction and obedience.
And think of the person who has been saying for months, “I’m still praying about it,” when you both know the real battle is fear.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But if Gospel-centered truth has strengthened you, you can help put that truth in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
That kind of support matters.

Invite your family. Invite the friend quietly struggling with faith. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks grace could never possibly be for someone like them.
Because fear has a way of returning with better arguments.
And when it does, come back and remember:
Waiting on God is holy when God has told you to wait.
But when His Word has already made obedience clear, fear does not become faith merely because we give it a spiritual name.
Jesus is not asking you to know the entire road.
He is calling you to trust the One who does.
And perhaps years from now, when you look back at the moment everything began to change, you will realize the miracle was not that God finally gave you another sign.
The miracle was that grace finally gave your trembling heart the courage to stop hiding and say yes to Jesus.
